FOREWORD
The  data  on  the  thermodynamic  and  transport  properties  are  essential  for  the  design,  performance  specifications  and  performance  analysis  of  boilers,  steam  turbines,  plant  process  and  other  mechanical  equipment  connected  with  power  generation.  With  a  view  to  present  thermodynamic  data  at  the  national  level,  catering to  the  need  of  Indian  power  industries,  the  Indian  Standards  Institution  published  Steam  Tables  in  1966.  The  Tables  contained  thermodynamic  properties  of  steam  in  the  range  of 0  to  800�C  temperature  and  0 to  500 kgf/cm2  pressure.  These Tables  were  more  or  less  a  reproduction  of  Vukalovich  Steam  Tables  1958;  which  were  based  on  Skeleton  Tables  available  till  1956.  Since  the  publication  of Vukalovich  Tables  1958,  considerable  progress  has  been  achieved  in  the  experimental  determination  and  analytical  representation  of  the  thermodynamic  properties  of water  and  steam.  As  a  result,  more  and  more reliable  experimental  data  were  made  available  in  wider  range  of pressure and  temperature.  The  Sixth  International  Conference  on  the  properties  of Steam  in  1963  approved  a  Skeleton  Table.  This  Skeleton  Table  was  derived  after  considering  all  the  data  submitted  by  various  member  countries.  The  need  was  felt,  at  that  time,  for  a  co relating  equation  to  represent  the  properties  conforming  with  the  Skeleton  Table  in  order  to  cater  to  the  computerized  calculations  in  the  industries.  An  International  Formulation  Committee  (IFC)  was  designated  for  preparing  the  formulation.  The  Committee  developed  the  1967  IFC  Formulation  for  industrial  use  and  the  1968  IFC  Formulation  for  scientific  and  general  uses.  These  formulations  were  approved  at  the  Seventh  International  Conference  in  1968.  The  two  formulations  generate  essentially  the  same  values  except  in  a  small  region  near  the  critical  point  where  the  1968  formulation  takes  care  of the  critical  region anomalies  to  a  certain  extent.  The  1967  IFC  Formulation  is  comparatively  simple  in  nature  for  programming  purposes  and  it  covers  all  the  regions  required  in  the  industrial  calculation.  The  ASME,  JSME,  VDI  and  UK  Steam  Tables  currently  in  circulation  were  prepared  using  the  1967  IFC  Formulation.  In  1979,  the  ISI  Subcommittee  for  the  preparation  of  Steam  Tables  decided  to  publish  new  Steam  Tables  by  adopting  the  1967  IFC  Formulation.  It  was  also  decided  to  incorporate  the  transport  properties  of  steam  to  be  prepared  in  accordance  with  the  latest  international  practices.  Since  our  country  adopted  SI  Units  through  the  standards  of  Weights  and  Measures  Act,  1976,  it  was  also  decided  to  bring  out  the  new  Steam  Tables  in  SI  Units.  The  thermodynamic  tables  have  been  calculated  using  the  1967  IFC  Formulations.  A  certain  amount  of  graphical  smoothing  was  done  in  case  of  isobaric  specific  heat  capacity.  The  data  on  dynamic  viscosity  was  prepared  using  the  '1975  IAPS*  Release  on  Dynamic  Viscosity',  and  the  data  on  thermal  conductivity  was  prepared  using  the '1977  IAPS  Release on Thermal Conductivity'.  The  formulation  and  the  data  on  surface  tension  was  prepared  using  the  '1975 
*The  International  Association  for  Properties  of  Steam  (IAPS)  is  the  permanent  organization  set  up. in  1968  to  coordinate  the  international  activities  on  the  properties  of  steam. 

IAPS Release on Surface Tension'. Values given in these IAPS Releases have been supplemented by the '1967 1FC Formulation' for the purpose of calculating the density. The member organizations of ISI Steam Tables Subcommittee took keen interest in bringing out the new edition of ISI Steam Tables. The Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited and Bhabha Atomic Research Centre took active part in preparing the Tables. The data was generated on the computer system at BHEL, Hardwar. The Committee is greatly indebted to BHEL, Hardwar, for the contribution of their members and for providing the computer facilities. The work on Mollier Diagrams in SI Units, which are considered necessary adjuncts to Steam Tables, is also on the programme of work of the ISI Subcommittee. This would be carried out using the computer aided plotting techniques. Bibliography 1. ASME Steam Tables (Fourth Edition); American Society of Mechanical Engineers, New York. 2. JSME Steam Table in SI-1980; Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers, Japan. 3. Properties of Water and Steam in SI Units-1969; Verein Deutscher Ingenieure, Dusseldorf.

ISI  STEAM  TABLES  IN  SI  UNITS 
1.  SCOPE  1.1  Steam Tables  in  SI  Units up to  100  MPa and  800�C  are  covered  in  this  publication.  There  are  thirteen  tables  in  all,  arranged  as  follows;  the  Tables  1  to  4  relate  to  the  thermodynamic  properties  and  the  rest  are  related  to  transport  properties  of  water  and  steam:  v  =  Specific  volume  m 3 /kg  h  =  Specific  enthalpy  kJ/kg  s  =  Specific  entropy  kJ/(kgK)  p  =  Density  kg/m 3  r  =  Heat  of  vapourization  kJ/kg  cp  =  Specific  heat  capacity  at  kJ/(kgK)  constant  pressure  �  =  Dynamic  viscosity  Pa.s  v  =  Kinematic  viscosity  m 2 /s    =  Thermal  conductivity  W/(m.K)    =  Thermal  diffusivity  m 2 /s  Pr  =  �cp/  =  Prandtl  number  N/m  a  =  Surface  tension  mm  a  =  Laplace  coefficient  Superscript  indicates  a  state  of  saturated  water.  Superscript  "  indicates  a  state  of  dry  saturated  steam.

For example,  when  the  coefficient  pressure  p  and  temperature  T  are  chosen  as  the  independent  variables  of  the  formulation,  then  2.  NOTATION  expressions  (here  called  derived  functions)  for  the  2.1  The  following  notations  have  been  used  in  specific  volume,  entropy,  enthalpy  and  all  other  thermodynamic  properties  may  be derived  directly  these  Tables:  by  partial  differentiation  of  the  socalled  t  =  Temperature  �C  canonical  (or  characteristic)  function  g  =  g  (p,  7),  T  =  t  +  273.15--Absolute  K  where  g  is  the  specific  free  enthalpy  (Gibbs  temperature  function).  Similarly,  when  the  specific  volume  v  and  temperature  T are  chosen  as  the  independent  p  =  Pressure  Pa  or  variables,  then  expressions  for  the  pressure,  mm Hg 
1 

SP : 26-1983 specific  entropy,  enthalpy  and  all  other  thermodynamic  properties  may be derived  directly  by  partial  differentiation  of  the  canonical  function  f  =  f  (v,  T),  where  f  is  the  specific  free  energy  (Helmholtz  function).  The  formulation  is  presented  in  terms  of  these  canonical  functions,  thereby  maintaining  thermodynamic  consistency.  The  canonical  functions  provide  the  definitive  expression  of  the  formulation.  The  derived  functions  are  for  practical  use  and  are  secondary  to  the  canonical  functions.  The  formulation  presented  herein  describes  the  thermodynamic  properties  of  ordinary  water  substance  throughout  the  whole  of the  region  that  extends  in  pressure  from  the  idealgas  limit  (at  zero  pressure)  to  a  pressure  of  108  N/m 2  (1000  bar),  and  that  extends  in  temperature  from  273.16  K  (0.01�C)  to  1073.15  K  (800�C).  This  whole  region  is  divided  into  six  sub regions,  numbered  1  to  6  and  shown  on  the  temperatureentropy  plane  in  Fig.  1  and  on  the  pressuretemperature  plane  in  Fig.  2.  The  entire  formulations  and  equations  have  been  split  up  in  the  following  groups:  a)  Physical  quantities,  quantity  symbols,  units  and  defined  constant  quantities  (3.1)  b)  Reduced  dimensionless  quantities  and  thermodynamic  relations  (3.2)  c)  Specification  of  the  subregions  (3.3)  d)  Subformulations  (3.4)  e)  The  Kfunction  (saturation  line)  (3.5)  f)  Canonical  functions  (3.6)  g)  Values  of the constants (3.7)  h)  Derived  constants  (3.8)  j)  Derived  functions  (3.9)  k)  Cautionary  notes (3.10) Brief descriptions  of this  grouping are as under,  but  the  same  have  been  dealt  in  details  later  (see 3.1  to 3.10). a) 3.1  lists  the  physical  quantities,  defines  the  quantity  symbols  and  units  used  in  the  for mulation,  and  defines  certain  constant  quantities  with  the  aid  of  which  the  expres sions  are  presented  in terms of reduced  dim ensionless  variables.  b) 3.2 presents the reduced dimensionless quan tities  and  also  the  required  thermodynamic  relations  by  means  of which  expressions  for  the  derived  functions  can  be  obtained  from  the  given  canonical  functions.  c) 3.3  specifies  the  subregions,  which  are  identified  by  numbers,  and  gives  informa tion  relating  to  equations  which  define  the  boundaries  between  subregions.  These  equations  are  identified  by  the  letters  K and  L,  the  Kfunction  being  the equation for the  saturation  line  and  the  Lfunction  being  the  equation  for  a  boundary  between  two  sub regions  in  the  singlephase  region.  d) 3.4  gives  the  specification  for  the  sub formulation  to  be  used  in  each  subregion.  Each  such  subformulation  comprises  the  canonical  function  relevant  to  the subregion,  together  with  derived  functions.  e) 3.5  presents  the  function  giving  the  satura tion  line,  which  also  serves  as  a  boundary  between  subregions.  This  function  is  identi fied  by  the  letter  K.  f) 3.6  presents  the  canonical  functions,  which  are  identified  by  the  letters  A,  B,  C  and  D.  The  canonical  parts  of the  subformulations  set  out  in 3.4  each  comprising  one  or  more  of  these  principal  canonical  functions.  g) 3.7  gives  the  values  of  the  constants  of  the  formulation.  Most  of  these  values  are  given  numerically;  a  few,  which  are  derived  from  other  constants,  are  given  symbolically.  The material in 3.1  to 3.7  is sufficient and  necessary  to  specify  the formulation.  h) 3.8  gives  the  numerical  values  of the derived  constants  and  a  derived  form  of the  Lfunc tion  convenient  for  computer  use.  j) 3.9  presents  those  derived  functions  which  are  of  practical  importance.  k) 3.10  gives information on the magnitudes of  small  discontinuities  in  property  values  which  occur  at  some  of  the  boundaries  between  subregions  and  draws  attention  to  the  need  for  caution  when  making  certain  calculations.  3.1 Physical Quantities, Quantity Symbols, Unite and Defined Constant Quantities 3.1.1  Physical  Quantities  (Properties) --  The  following  physical  quantities  are  given  the

(1) The specific internal energy is m a de exactly zero for the liquid phase at the triple point. (2) The states here shown are metastable. (3) At a pressure of exactly 1.013 25 bar the saturation temperature has the exact assigned value of 100�C on the International Practical Scale of Temperature, 1948. At a temperature of exactly 100�C on the Thermodynamic Celsius Scale the saturation pressure is 1.013 25 bar, with a tolerance of 0.000 04 bar. (4) Near the critical point, the tolerances on the specific volume and on the specific enthalpy in the vapor phase are correlated with the corresponding tolerances in the liquid phase. The tolerances on the changes in specific volume and in specific enthalpy on evaporation tend to zero as the critical point is approached.
